lessons.title: -உக்கு (-ukku) — "to, for"
lessons.gloss: the dative suffix -ukku, 'to / for,' including its two surface forms and irregular enakku

segments.text: Your first case ending. English says "to me" with a separate word in front. Tamil says it with a piece stuck on the back — and that small difference is the biggest structural fact about the language.
Take a noun you know and add -உக்கு (-ukku):

utterances: word: பெயர் peyar — name. + the dative: பெயருக்கு peyarukku. meaning: to/for the name.
word: வேலை vēlai — work. + the dative: வேலைக்கு vēlaikku. meaning: for work.

segments.text: The suffix has two shapes — -உக்கு -ukku and -க்கு -kku — chosen by the sound the noun ends in. One case, two forms; the seam still shows.
And with "I" — this one is irregular and worth memorising, because you'll use it constantly:
நான் nāṉ ("I") becomes எனக்கு enakku ("to me").
The pronoun changes its body (nāṉ becomes en-) before the suffix lands. Nouns don't — they just take the ending.

What does -உக்கு mean? ("To" or "for.") Where does it go? (On the end of the noun — Tamil adds, it doesn't put a word in front.) What is "to me"? (எனக்கு enakku — the pronoun's body changes to en- first.) Why does the suffix show up as -ukku and -kku? (One case, two shapes, chosen by the noun's ending.) Next: two more letters — ம and retroflex ண.

lessons.title: ம and ண — a loop, and a curled tongue
lessons.gloss: write ம and retroflex ண while training the tongue to curl back

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ம, Script you'll notice: ண and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Two more letters, and with them you'll have every letter of this book's first word. One is easy. The other is a sound you may not be able to hear yet.
a straight vertical stroke on the LEFT.
a horizontal along the bottom.
a rounded arch closing it on the RIGHT.

Get the sides the right way round. The upright is on the left and the curve on the right — which is the reverse of what most people guess, and the reverse of the Devanagari habit of hanging a shape off a right-hand spine.
a straight top bar.
a loop on the left.
two arches.
a straight vertical on the right, down to the baseline.
The dot under the romanization — ṇ, not plain n — is doing real work.
Say English n. Your tongue touches just behind your teeth.
Now curl the tip of your tongue up and back toward the roof of your mouth, and say it again. That is ṇ, and it is a different letter in Tamil.

English has no such sound and no way to write one, which is why an English speaker typically cannot hear the difference at first. That is expected. The ear learns it after the hand does, which is one good argument for writing the letters rather than only reading them.

Retroflex sounds are a signature of the languages of India — they show up across Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Hindi and Sanskrit alike, in families that are otherwise unrelated to each other. It's one of the features that makes South Asia a linguistic area: neighbouring languages that borrowed a sound from each other rather than inheriting it.

segments.instruction: ண — "top bar, left loop, two arches, straight vertical"
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: ண — "top bar, left loop, **two** arches, straight vertical"]

segments.instruction: plain n, then curl the tongue back — ṇ
segments.source: [YOU SAY: plain *n*, then curl the tongue back — **ṇ**]

segments.text: Draw ம — which side is the upright on? (The left; the arch closes it on the right.) Draw ண — what makes it not ன? (One extra arch: ண has two arches where ன has one. Both end in the same straight vertical.) What does the dot in ṇ mean? (Retroflex — the tongue curls back to the roof of the mouth.) Why can't you hear it yet? (English has no such sound; the ear learns it after the hand.) Next: stacking that dative suffix where Latin would fuse several meanings.

lessons.title: -உக்கு (-ukku) — one carriage in a suffix train
lessons.gloss: Tamil stacks a visible one-purpose dative suffix where Latin fuses several meanings

segments.text: You can point to peyar and -ukku separately. That visible seam is the structural lesson.

utterances: fixes the case? Tamil -ukku: dative, always. Latin -īs: dative or ablative.
carries number? Tamil -ukku: no; another suffix can. Latin -īs: plural is baked in.
carries declension? Tamil -ukku: no. Latin -īs: first/second class is baked in.
visible seam? Tamil -ukku: peyar + ukku. Latin -īs: one fused ending.

segments.text: Tamil stacks. Each suffix contributes one meaning in a fixed order, like a train carriage. Latin fuses case, number, and class into an indivisible ending, and -īs does not even identify one case by itself.
This is agglutinative structure: long words remain buildable because their pieces stay legible. The comparison is not about simplicity; it is about where the grammatical information lives.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "one suffix, one meaning, visible seam"]

segments.text: What does -ukku contribute? (Dative to/for, one meaning.) What does Latin -īs fuse? (Case, plural number, and declension class.) Which system leaves the seam visible? (Tamil's agglutinative stack.)

lessons.title: எனக்குத் தமிழ் தெரியும் (enakkut tamiḻ teriyum) — "I know Tamil"
lessons.gloss: 'I know Tamil' — built with no subject, because knowing happens TO you

segments.text: In Chapter 5 you said நான் தமிழ் பேசுகிறேன் — "I speak Tamil," with nāṉ as the subject. Now say "I know Tamil." Tamil will not let you use nāṉ.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The sentence

segments.text: எனக்குத் தமிழ் தெரியும் (enakkut tamiḻ teriyum). enakku tamiḻ teriyum. literally: "to-me Tamil is-known."
Word by word:

utterances: piece: எனக்கு(த்) enakku(t), "to me" — the dative from the last lesson.
piece: தெரியும் teriyum, "is known / is apparent".

segments.text: That extra த் on enakku is sandhi — a joining consonant Tamil inserts between certain words to smooth the seam. It belongs to neither word on its own; it exists only because they are next to each other. Nothing to learn yet, but worth noticing, because you will see it constantly.

You are not the subject. Nāṉ is gone — the person has been moved into the dative. What's left in the plain, unmarked form is tamiḻ: the sentence is now about the language, and you are merely the one it is known to.
(Grammarians call enakku the dative subject, because it behaves like the subject even though it isn't in the subject case. The odd feeling of the sentence is exactly that split.)

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: Why: things that happen to you

segments.text: Tamil sorts verbs by whether you do something or something happens to you. Speaking is something you do — so Ch. 5 used nāṉ. But knowing, liking, wanting, being hungry, being cold: these arrive at you. Tamil marks that by putting the person in the dative.

utterances: English frames it as: I know Tamil. Tamil frames it as: Tamil is known to me.
English frames it as: I like it. Tamil frames it as: it is pleasing to me.
English frames it as: I am cold. Tamil frames it as: cold is to me.

segments.text: English does this occasionally and archaically — "methinks" is exactly it (me is dative: "it seems to me"). Tamil made it a rule.

segments.instruction: the contrast — "nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ" (I speak) … "enakku tamiḻ teriyum" (known to me)
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the contrast — "*nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ*" (I speak) … "*enakku tamiḻ teriyum*" (known to me)]

segments.text: What does எனக்குத் தமிழ் தெரியும் (enakkut tamiḻ teriyum) literally say? ("To-me Tamil is-known.") Which word has English got that Tamil hasn't? (A nominative "I" — nāṉ is replaced by the dative enakku.) Why does Tamil use the dative here? (Because knowing happens to you; you don't do it.) Which English word preserves the same idea? (Methinks — "it seems to me".) Next: watch all four Dravidian sisters use the same experiencer shape.

lessons.title: -ukku, -ku, -ge, -ikku — the family shows its bones
lessons.gloss: all four Dravidian sisters put the experiencer in visibly related dative forms

segments.text: Tamil says knowing happens to you. Its three closest sisters make the same grammatical choice.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: Four sentences, one construction

utterances: language: Tamil. "I know [the language]": enakku tamiḻ teriyum. dative: -ukku.
language: Telugu. "I know [the language]": nāku telugu vaccu. dative: -ku.
language: Kannada. "I know [the language]": nanage kannaḍa gottu. dative: -ge.
language: Malayalam. "I know [the language]": enikku malayāḷam aṟiyām. dative: -ikku.

segments.text: The verbs differ, but the experiencer sits in a dative whose forms visibly belong together: -ukku / -ku / -ge / -ikku. This is family evidence, just as blanc/bianco/branco exposes Romance kinship.
The comparison also makes cross-language practice useful: once you recognize "to me," you can search for the known or apparent thing rather than forcing an English subject onto the sentence.

segments.source: [YOU POINT: the experiencer in each sentence]
[YOU PARAPHRASE: "the language is known to me"]

segments.text: Do the four sisters agree on dative experiencers? (Yes.) Which four suffix shapes reveal the relationship? (-ukku, -ku, -ge, -ikku.) What stays plain in the sentence? (The thing known or experienced.)

lessons.title: ந, ன, ண (na, ṉa, ṇa) — three stops on one tongue-map
lessons.gloss: Tamil writes dental, alveolar, and retroflex n with three separate letters

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
waitUntilStopped: Script you'll notice: The backward walk
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: The backward walk and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: English writes one n. Tamil keeps three tongue positions apart.

blocks.title: Script you'll notice: The backward walk

utterances: letter: ந. sound: na. tongue: against the teeth (dental).
letter: ன. sound: ṉa. tongue: on the ridge behind the teeth (alveolar).
letter: ண. sound: ṇa. tongue: curled back to the roof (retroflex).

segments.text: Move backward: teeth becomes ridge becomes curled roof. English spells all three with one letter and initially hears them as the same sound; Tamil uses separate letters because its words depend on the contrast.

You will draw ந and ன when nandri needs them. For now compare the last pair: ண is ன with one extra arch. Both open with a top bar and loop and finish with the same vertical. ன has one middle arch; ண has two.

Retroflex sounds occur across unrelated South Asian language families. That shared geography makes the region a linguistic area: neighbors can borrow a sound pattern without inheriting it from one ancestor.
